body_markdown:
Nostalgia is a heavy lens through which to judge a motor car. The classic Japanese car market has long been captivated by the cinematic mystique and PlayStation provenance of the Subaru Impreza 22B. It is a stunning thing to behold, a blistered, wide-arched homage to[Colin McRae](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/watch-this-epic-onboard-footage-of-colin-mcrae-from-2001/) that now comfortably inhabits the[$150,000—$250,000 valuation realm](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/subaru/impreza/1998/1998-subaru-impreza-22b~sti?id=aCn1I000000DCIuSAO) , with exceptional cars having gone much further still. But is the 22B the best Impreza? Hmmm…


If you want the ultimate Subaru Impreza—and frankly, the finest rally replica ever created—you must look past the 22B. Past the Ford Escort RS Cosworth with its charming but distinctly old-school power delivery, past the Lancia Delta Integrale Evo II with its well-documented delicacy. You must even look respectfully past the almighty[Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VI Tommi Mäkinen Edition](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/auctions/can-this-mitsubishi-lancer-tommi-makinen-jump-higher-than-100100/) . The apex of the breed is something known largely only to the JDM hardcore—a late second-generation “Hawkeye” Impreza with a name so comically long it barely fits on a title: Subaru Impreza WRX STI Spec C Type RA-R.


Subaru


Subaru


To understand the RA-R, you have to understand the anorak-level minutiae of Subaru’s motorsport division, Subaru Tecnica International. The standard STI was the fast road car. The Spec C, or Specification Competition, was the Group N homologation lightweight, stripped of mass and sharpened for rallying. The Type RA, or Record Attempt, added still more focus. But for this swansong of the Hawkeye generation, Subaru Tecnica International added an extra R, officially for “radical” or “racy.” Effectively, Subaru took the homologation special, handed it to the motorsport engineers and told them to build the sharpest tarmac weapon in the company’s history.


Let’s start with the elephant in the room: the aesthetic. To the uninitiated, the RA-R looks almost naked. There is no towering rear wing and no visual theater for people who need their homologation specials to shout across a supermarket parking lot. It was offered in Pure White, WR Rally Blue Mica, and a special run of just 50 Astral Yellow cars, but the shape itself is comically discreet. From the rear it looks almost apologetic, as if someone has nicked the spoiler off a proper STI. This was not a styling oversight. The RA-R was not a dress-up special. It was a road-going precision instrument built around response, weight, grip, and stiffness rather than rally-rep pantomime. For the discerning street driver, that created the ultimate stealth silhouette, though many have since sprouted wings.


Subaru


But beneath that unassuming, wingless body lies a chassis of magnificent, scalpel-sharp capability. Where a standard Impreza, even a base Spec C, has a degree of inherent road-going compliance, the RA-R was subjected to a comprehensive kinematic overhaul. STI binned the ordinary softness and fitted reinforced dampers, springs, and stabilizers, with the ride height hunkered down over special 18-inch wheels. Crucially, it replaced the rubber suspension bushings with pillow-ball joints throughout the suspension links.


If you have driven a standard Hawkeye STI, you know it is a rapid, capable thing, but without some of the fizz of an Integrale, even if the Impreza is empirically the more accomplished car—as it should be, since it’s far newer. But climbing into an RA-R is a revelation. You genuinely feel the difference within the first 50 yards. That extra R brings an astonishing level of brilliance to your inputs. The pillow-ball joints eradicate all the slack from the chassis; the steering is telepathic and reacts to micro-adjustments with a ferocity that makes a Delta Integrale feel almost laid-back by comparison. Braking, courtesy of special six-pot front Brembo calipers biting into slotted discs, is violent enough to detach your retinas.


Subaru


Subaru


Then there is the engine. It is the accepted wisdom that the Evo VI TME is the king of the rally reps, but the Evo demands you drive it with absolute commitment everywhere to feel that magic. If you don’t … well, it’s a four-cylinder four-door sedan; it only truly comes alive when you have it by the scruff of the neck. The RA-R is different. At its heart is the 2.0-liter EJ20 derived from the limited-edition WRX STI S204, which is widely reported to have been hand-balanced and blueprinted, fed by a larger twin-scroll, ball-bearing turbocharger with optimized turbine-blade design.


The JDM twin-scroll EJ20 architecture uses equal-length exhaust manifolding, so do not come here expecting the traditional loping Subaru burble. That would rather miss the point. The result is an engine that produces 316 horsepower, and a muscular 318 pound-feet of torque, but it does so with an emotional pull that entirely shatters the clinical Japanese car myth. It does not burble; it emits a hard, frantic, metallic motorsport scream as it races to its 8000-rpm redline. Yet you do not need to be driving at ten-tenths to feel the joy of this powertrain. It is infinitely flexible, yet utterly intoxicating when provoked. It may not have the fairy-dust connection of McRae or Richard Burns, but thread an RA-R down a wet back road, and you will feel every inch the WRC god. If you just want to drive with a wee bit of verve, there’s theater aplenty to make any journey entertaining, if not exactly a luxury experience.


Subaru


So, how do you go about owning the best Impreza ever made? It requires a leap of faith, because the RA-R was produced exclusively for the Japanese domestic market, and just 300 units were built in 2006.


The reality of ownership is a double-edged sword: On one hand, it is a Hawkeye Impreza, and every competent Japanese performance specialist in the country can change a cam belt, diagnose an EJ20 misfire, or source a clutch. However, the RA-R-specific parts, those glorious six-pot Brembos, the STI suspension components, and the unique 18-inch wheels, are ruinously expensive and incredibly difficult to source outside Japan.


Importing one is your primary hurdle. First and foremost, the 25-year import rule works against this 20-year-old car. There are undoubtedly hoops to jump through for a[show-and-display](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/this-jaguar-set-the-tone-for-importing-under-show-or-display/) exemption, and the RA-R isn’t even on the list of approved cars (though one could try to make the case), so otherwise you’re looking at 2031. When the time has come, however, you will need to employ a reputable importer to scour Japan for a good example. Right now, the RA-R still represents a great bargain in Japanese performance. In the U.K., recent evidence suggests usable cars in the $40K–$70K range, with condition, mileage, originality, and color doing serious damage to the final number. A really sharp example, especially in Astral Yellow, is now easily a $60K–$80K proposition. It’s probably safe to assume these prices will only increase in the coming years.


Still, compare them to the six-figure sums now required to buy a gorgeous, but dynamically older 22B. For a third of the price of the museum piece, you have a genuinely rare homologation special that demands no apologies. It is the zenith of the analog, mechanical rally replica, and proof positive that the longest name in the business absolutely belongs to the best rally-rep in the world.


Yes, you can put a spoiler on them.


Subaru
